opus-5.5.text:
Oh, massively. DeepStack was probably the single paper that pulled me into this whole field. I was still in high school when it came out, and I remember reading it and feeling like something clicked. Up until then, most of what I'd seen in game-playing AI was about perfect-information games like chess or Go, where you can see the whole board. Poker is different: you don't know what cards the other person holds, so you have to reason about beliefs, about ranges, about what your opponent thinks you might have. DeepStack showed that you could combine search with learned intuition, a neural network that estimates the value of a situation, in a setting with hidden information, and actually beat professional players at heads-up no-limit.

What struck me most wasn't even the poker result itself. It was the idea underneath it: that you don't have to precompute a strategy for every possible situation. You can reason on the fly, look ahead a bit, and lean on a learned value function to cut off the search. That combination of search plus learning felt like a much more general recipe than "train a giant policy and hope it generalizes."

So I spent a lot of my early research time in that world: counterfactual regret minimization, deep variants of it, trying to make these methods scale without hand-crafted abstractions. A lot of what I believe today about how to build systems that actually reason, rather than just pattern-match, traces back to that period. The intuition that you want a model that can spend more compute at test time to think harder about a hard problem, that came straight out of game AI for me. DeepStack was where I first saw it work in a really messy, adversarial, imperfect-information setting, and I've been chasing some version of that idea ever since.

r001.rationale: The response describes DeepStack as a major influence on Eric’s early research and current ideas, but it does not characterize its influence on his personal development as greater than its influence on his current work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, DeepStack was the paper that changed the trajectory of my life. I was a teenager when it came out, and I remember reading it and just being stunned. Before that, the dominant approach to poker was to solve this giant abstraction of the game offline and then look up your strategy at the table. DeepStack flipped that around. It said: don't try to solve everything up front, instead reason about the situation you're actually in, right now, and use a learned value function to tell you what the future looks like. That's search plus learning, which is the same recipe AlphaGo used, but doing it in an imperfect information game was so much harder, and they pulled it off.

What got me wasn't just the result, it was that it felt like a way of thinking. It made me believe that these games weren't these impossible things reserved for big labs, that if you understood the math and were stubborn enough, you could actually build it. So I did. I spent probably two years essentially re-deriving and reimplementing that line of work, first my own version of the algorithms, then the follow-ups from Noam Brown and Tuomas Sandholm with Libratus and Pluribus, and I open sourced a lot of that. That whole period taught me how to do research, how to read a paper and not just take the headline but understand every design decision and why it had to be that way.

And the deeper influence is still with me today. The idea that you want a system that can think at inference time, that scales its reasoning with the difficulty of the problem instead of just memorizing a policy, that's basically the thesis I've been chasing ever since, now with language models instead of poker. So I'd say DeepStack didn't just influence me, it kind of set the whole direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes DeepStack as shaping Eric’s research skills and setting his direction, while also connecting its ideas to his current language-model work. It does not say its influence was greater on his personal development than on his current work.

astra-6.text:
DeepStack was a huge inspiration for me. It showed that you could combine deep learning with search to make progress in poker, where you don’t get to see the full state of the world. You have to reason about what the other player might know and what they might do.

What I found compelling was the idea that you don’t need a neural network to solve everything on its own. You can use it to guide computation at decision time. That combination really shaped how I thought about AI and the kinds of problems I wanted to work on.
